current_answer: Platform conversation logs can make an occupation look more or less exposed to AI partly because of who uses that platform. A 2026 methodological preprint held its U.S. employment design fixed and changed only the platform input: some estimates reversed sign, and workforce reweighting reduced coefficient magnitudes by 42–93%. This does not prove that AI has no employment effect; the exercise diagnoses a measurement problem in platform-derived exposure. Separate studies still report narrow early-career hiring warnings, mixed pay results and no clear economy-wide U.S. job-loss footprint. Those findings use different populations and measures.

catalogue_card.question: Can AI-use logs misstate job risk?
catalogue_card.text: A fixed U.S. employment analysis changed sign when researchers changed only which AI platform supplied usage data. That is a warning about the exposure measure, not proof that AI has no effect on jobs.

summary: A May 2026 methodological preprint compares platform-derived exposure scores under one fixed U.S. employment design.
Switching the conversation-share input changed estimated employment coefficients; consumer and enterprise channels within one vendor disagreed in sign.
Reweighting platform users to the workforce occupation mix reduced coefficient magnitudes by 42–93% across tested specifications.
This is a measurement diagnostic, not an estimate of jobs lost or saved by AI.
uncertainty: The platform-selection test is a May 2026 preprint newly added to this map, not a new September labor outcome or a causal estimate of AI-driven employment change.
Its sensitivity result applies to exposure scores built with platform conversation shares; it does not invalidate every task-capability, survey, adoption or administrative measure.
Workforce reweighting addresses observed occupation mix, not all within-occupation selection or non-AI confounders.
freshness_note: Checked 30 September 2026. Added a platform-exposure measurement warning; previous outcome findings remain separately scoped.
